comments.text: i don't think you've adequately distinguished between the peak, but easily scheduled energy demands of AI training, and the lower but absolutely inflexible firm energy demands of AI inference. or the difference between the high speed fiber connections that need to exist within a data center for the former purpose, and the proximity to the end user for the latter. if centers specialized, then proximity to steady energy generation and to urban centers would be critical for inference centers, whereas AI training centers would be best situated wherever it is cheapest to both cool them and to use massive amounts of off-peak energy - which at this stage in history can be accomplished with renewables and battery storage in a rural area. the problem is that it would be a wasteful investment in an AI data center for it to be idling when not training, so centers use their GPUs for both. but there is a geographic and function allocation optimization problem to solve here that isn't as simple as "AI needs to be near reliable baseload" - the functions that demand the most instantaneous power are not the ones that need an uninterrupted supply or that need any proximity to end users !

replies.text:
Fair hit, and you'd know better than I would. That line is Steve Gaitten's own recollection from an Ashburn Magazine retrospective on AOL, and I quoted it without flagging that it's one guy's memory of a drive 27 years earlier. Herndon, Sterling Park and Dulles were all very much there in 1996.

The thing his memory gets right is the scale. Loudoun had 86,000 people in 1990 and 170,000 by 2000. Ashburn itself was about 3,400 people in the 1990 census, against roughly 43,000 by 2010. And the building AOL bought at Route 28 and Waxpool was the old British Aerospace place, which had been sitting largely empty since BAe decided not to expand there.

So: established towns, yes. A built-out corridor, not yet.
